title: Who sweeps a room
hook: Herbert's The Elixir: sweeping a room for God makes it fine
carry: makes that and the action fine
tomorrow: a cook kept forgetting God all day. what did he do about it?

segments.voice: Yesterday Herbert called prayer a banquet, a breath going home, and something understood. Same poet today. Different room of the house.

The scrape of a broom. Grit under your shoes in the kitchen. A dish rack that refills the second you empty it. Chores are the part of the day nobody posts. So what could turn sweeping a dusty floor into gold? George Herbert has an answer, and he put it in a poem called The Elixir, after the stone that old stories said could turn plain metal into gold. His stone isn't in a lab. It's a short phrase.
screen: `THE SCRAPE OF A BROOM.` → `THE PART NOBODY POSTS.` → `A STONE THAT TURNS THINGS TO GOLD.`

segments.voice: The poem opens as a request: "Teach me, my God and King, In all things thee to see, And what I do in any thing, To do it as for thee." As for thee. That's the phrase. Then Herbert walks into the plainest room in the house. "A servant with this clause Makes drudgery divine: Who sweeps a room, as for thy laws, Makes that and th' action fine." Look at what changes. Not the broom. Not the dust. Not the room. The reason. Same strokes, done for someone, and Herbert says two things become fine: the room, and the act of sweeping it. Then he names his secret: "This is the famous stone That turneth all to gold." He's leaning on Paul, who told the Colossians: "whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men." There's a picture in the poem for how this works, too. You can look at a window and stop at the glass, smudges and all. Or you can look through it, and the poem says then the heavens come into view. Sweeping is the glass. One to tell a friend: Herbert's word for drudgery and his word for divine sit side by side in one line.
screen: `AS FOR THEE.` · `WHO SWEEPS A ROOM.` · `THE ROOM AND THE ACTION, FINE.` · `LOOK THROUGH THE GLASS.` · then, large: `MAKES THAT AND THE ACTION FINE.`

segments.voice: Take a broom, or a cloth if there's no broom nearby, and clean one small patch: a step, a counter, a corner. Go slowly, one stroke on each out-breath, and listen to the bristles. Do it as for someone: for God if you pray, for the next person who walks there if you don't.
Who sweeps a room. Herbert's plainest chore, done as for thee, and turned to gold without changing a single stroke.
Your line: makes that and the action fine. The broom stays a broom; the reason changes. Day 1656, swept.

howItsDone: Herbert's The Elixir is sung as the hymn 'Teach me, my God and King' in some churches; many Christians draw on Colossians 3:23 to treat ordinary work as done for God.

chat.says: Pop's in rehab. i do his dishes and laundry daily. bye senior spring. it's just chores, right?
options: Herbert says sweeping a room as for someone makes the action fine. Same dishes, different reason.
Chores aren't prayer. Get them done fast so you can get back to things that matter.
Only if you pray out loud while you do them; otherwise it's just housework.
chat.meaning: In The Elixir, the clause 'as for thee' changes the reason, not the work: who sweeps a room makes that and the action fine.
